sections.title: One medium, several speakers
sections.narration: Picture a group discussion where everyone shares one microphone. Who gets to speak now? Networks have the same kind of problem. Medium access control sets the rules for using a shared connection, not for choosing an Internet route.
sections.takeaway: Medium access control decides how stations share a communication resource.

sections.title: Make overlap visible
sections.narration: A and C both start before either hears the other. Their signals meet, and the transmissions fail in this shared-link example. The red disturbance spreads back. Talking louder won't fix this group discussion; we need better rules.
bullets: A receiver may lose both frames
sections.takeaway: A collision concerns overlapping signals at a receiver.

sections.title: Pure ALOHA: send when ready
sections.narration: Pure ALOHA has a very simple rule: if you have data, send it. No common starting slots. That freedom comes with a catch: transmissions can overlap, and a failed attempt may need to be tried again later.
sections.takeaway: Pure ALOHA allows a station to begin transmitting whenever data is ready.

sections.title: A vulnerable interval of 2T
sections.narration: Suppose one frame lasts T. Another frame can cause trouble by starting within T before it or T after it starts. Put those two risky intervals together, and the total window is two T.
bullets: Conflicts can start before or after
sections.takeaway: For equal-length pure ALOHA frames, the vulnerable interval spans 2T.

sections.title: Why retry randomly?
sections.narration: If both stations retry after exactly the same wait, they may crash into each other again. Choosing different random waits helps separate the attempts. It improves our chances, but it isn't a promise of success next time.
bullets: Identical waits can repeat a clash
sections.takeaway: Independent retry timing reduces the chance of repeated collisions.

sections.title: Slotted ALOHA adds boundaries
sections.narration: Slotted ALOHA adds a shared clock: start only at slot boundaries. Two stations can still choose the same slot and collide. But now slightly different start times can't create quite the same messy overlap as before.
sections.takeaway: Slotted ALOHA restricts transmission starts to common slot boundaries.

sections.title: The vulnerable interval becomes T
sections.narration: With equal-size frames fitting the slots, only attempts in the same slot conflict. Our risky interval drops from two T to T. A little timing agreement makes a big difference to the possible clashes.
sections.takeaway: Under the ideal slot model, the vulnerable interval is one slot.

sections.title: Interpret the ideal efficiency result
sections.narration: Watch more stations try sending. In the ideal model, pure ALOHA peaks around eighteen point four percent; slotted reaches thirty-six point eight. Beyond that, extra attempts create extra collisions. More effort can mean less useful work.
sections.takeaway: The familiar ALOHA maxima depend on a specific ideal traffic model.

sections.title: Scheduling or contention?
sections.narration: There are two broad plans: reserve turns with a schedule, or let stations compete for a chance. Either way, the connection has limited capacity. We still need rules so everyone isn't trying to use the same space together.
sections.takeaway: Collision reduction comes with assumptions or coordination costs.

sections.title: Listen before transmitting
sections.narration: Before speaking, listen. That's the basic idea of carrier sensing. If the channel sounds busy, wait according to your rules. It's an improvement over sending blindly, though we'll soon see why listening doesn't solve every collision.
bullets: Defer when the channel is busy
sections.takeaway: Carrier sensing can avoid transmissions that obviously conflict locally.

sections.title: A distant sender can still start
sections.narration: Here's the catch: signals need time to travel. A distant station may hear silence just after another has started. Both can honestly think the channel is free. The problem is delay, not that someone forgot to listen.
bullets: Both ends may initially sense idle
sections.takeaway: Propagation delay allows collisions even with carrier sensing.

sections.title: One-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: One-persistent CSMA keeps listening and sends as soon as the channel becomes idle. Nice and eager. But if several stations have been waiting, they may all jump in at once, like a class answering the same question.
bullets: Transmit when the medium becomes idle
sections.takeaway: One-persistent stations transmit as soon as their sensed channel becomes idle.

sections.title: Nonpersistent CSMA
sections.narration: Nonpersistent CSMA takes a short random break after finding the channel busy, then checks again. That can prevent everyone restarting together. The trade-off? Sometimes the channel sits empty while stations are still taking their little breaks.
sections.takeaway: Nonpersistent waiting reduces synchronized attempts but can add idle delay.

sections.title: P-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: With p-persistent CSMA, an idle slot becomes a probability choice. Send with probability p; otherwise, wait for another chance. This assumes a suitable slot-based setup. The goal is to spread out attempts instead of having everyone rush in.
sections.takeaway: P-persistent CSMA makes a probabilistic choice at an idle slot.

sections.title: Add detection on historical Ethernet
sections.narration: Now we're looking at older shared, half-duplex Ethernet. CSMA/CD listens before sending and checks for collisions while sending. Keep that setting in mind: this isn't how every modern Ethernet link works, and it isn't Wi-Fi's rulebook.
sections.takeaway: CSMA/CD belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not all modern Ethernet links.

sections.title: Detect, abort, and signal
sections.narration: A collision is detected, so stop that unsuccessful frame, send the jam signal, and back off. The spreading red signal helps make the failure known. Then the stations can wait before trying again with fresh timing.
sections.takeaway: Collision detection limits time wasted on an already failed transmission.

sections.title: Why propagation affects frame length
sections.narration: A far-end collision can't be reported instantly. The signal travels out, then the information travels back. The sender must still be transmitting to detect it. That's why frame time and network size are linked in shared Ethernet.
bullets: A far-end clash must return in time
sections.takeaway: Collision detection constrains the relation between frame time and network extent.
sections.short_title: The collision must return in time

sections.title: Widen the random retry range
sections.narration: Repeated collisions? Widen the choice of random waits: two options, then four, then eight. That's binary exponential backoff. We're giving attempts more room to spread out, not handing every station a permanent turn on the line.
sections.takeaway: Binary exponential backoff expands the retry-choice range after collisions.

sections.title: Work two retry choices
sections.narration: After the first collision, choose zero or one slot. After the second, choose zero through three. Different choices create different waits. Like leaving the classroom at slightly different times, that makes another pile-up less likely.
sections.takeaway: After two collisions, this example draws independently from four slot choices.

sections.title: Backoff does not reserve the cable
sections.narration: Finishing your wait doesn't mean the channel now belongs to you. Someone else may already be sending. You still need to follow the sensing rules. A backoff timer is a waiting plan, not a reservation slip.
sections.takeaway: Finishing a backoff does not guarantee exclusive access.
sections.short_title: Backoff does not reserve a turn

sections.title: Modern switched full duplex
sections.narration: Now the setup changes. Switched full-duplex links have separate sending and receiving paths, so opposite flows can travel together. The old shared-wire collision problem is gone on these links, and they don't use CSMA/CD.
sections.takeaway: Full-duplex switched Ethernet removes the shared-wire collision scenario.

sections.title: Wi-Fi needs different feedback
sections.narration: Wi-Fi has its own complications. A station doesn't simply do Ethernet-style collision detection while transmitting. Here, the access point receives data and sends feedback. Avoiding clashes and receiving acknowledgments matter, especially when stations can't hear the same things.
bullets: Avoidance and ACKs help manage access
sections.takeaway: Wi-Fi uses collision-avoidance mechanisms rather than Ethernet-style CSMA/CD.

sections.title: Compare the added knowledge
sections.narration: Look at how the rules build up. ALOHA sends; CSMA listens first; CSMA/CD also detects collisions in its shared-wire setting. Each method gets more information, but none makes signals travel instantly or gives unlimited space to everyone.
sections.takeaway: Each improvement adds information while retaining physical limitations.

sections.title: Explain the next collision
sections.narration: When you see the next transmission, ask three questions: what can this station hear, when is it allowed to start, and how does it retry? Answer those, and the long protocol names become much easier to explain.
sections.takeaway: Medium-access behavior depends on both protocol rules and physical context.
